newsitem.title: GERMANY: Hamburg crusher backs modified U.S. soybeans.
newsitem.headline: Hamburg crusher backs modified U.S. soybeans.

text.p: Major European seed crusher Oelmuehle Hamburg AG backed imports of genetically- modified soybeans from the U.S. from late 1996, board chairman Arnd von Wissel said.
"We advocate the introduction of these new soybeans but it has to be done in conjunction with good consumer education measures," he told a shareholders' meeting on Wednesday.
"We aim at providing our customers with all the necessary information to answer consumers' questions and to pre-empt possible fears."
Von Wissels said European crushers needed to secure soybean supplies in international markets and therefore needed to embrace new product trends.
But it was uncertain how consumers would react to the new product and this overshadowed business expectations for 1996.
Herbicide-resistant soybeans named "Roundup Ready" are estimated to account for one or two percent of the expected U.S. crop this year.
Developed by chemicals firm Monsanto Co, they are resistant to Monsanto's "Roundup" herbicide, so that herbicides can be used more selectively and sparingly.
This may cut farmers' costs and reduce ecological damage.
The EU in April approved imports of these beans and is studying applications for the sale of herbicide-resistant domestic rapeseed. Canada has already approved such rape crops.
Von Wissel said he had assurances from U.S. growers that a separation of the new soybeans and those produced traditionally was impossible in both storage and transport.

He shared the belief a separation was unnecessary because the health and safety procedures in the U.S., at EU level, and in individual EU member states had tested the products and ruled that health and environmetal risks could be excluded.
Oelmuehle last year crushed two million tonnes of soybeans out of a total 3.4 million tonne German crush.
An American Soybean Association (ASA) delegation to Hamburg on Monday stressed "Roundup Ready" product qualities were identical with those of traditional soybeans.
ASA chief executive officer told Reuters, "These beans are safe...we want to reach out to the consumer to get that message across."
Censky said ASA would provide European customers with the promotional and educational guidelines. --Vera Eckert, Hamburg newsroom, +49-40-41903275
